page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Two solutions that have the same osmotic
pressure at the same temperature are called
When they are separated by a semi-permeable
membrane there is no net flow of solvent in
steps.why: Osmosis is driven by a difference in osmotic pressure. If two solutions have the same osmotic pressure there is no difference to drive the flow, so the volumes on the two sides stay as they are. That is the whole content of the word isotonic.
common_mistakes: Saying isotonic means the same concentration by mass. It means the same osmotic pressure, which depends on the number of particles.
Leaving out "at the same temperature". Osmotic pressure changes with temperature, so the comparison is only valid at one temperature.
steps.memory_tip: Same osmotic pressure on both sides, so no net flow across the membrane.
steps.margin_note: The marked words are "same osmotic pressure". Adding "at the same temperature" completes the line.

steps.label: Example and the two other cases
lines: This is why 0.9% saline is used for
A solution of HIGHER osmotic pressure than
A solution of LOWER osmotic pressure is
steps.why: The example is the reason the term is taught: a fluid injected into blood must not move water into or out of the red blood cells. In a hypertonic solution water leaves the cells and they shrink; in a hypotonic solution water enters and the cells swell and may burst. Only the isotonic solution leaves them unchanged.
common_mistakes: Writing 0.9% NaCl with no (w/v). The figure is a mass of NaCl per volume of solution, so the unit label is part of the answer.
Swapping hypertonic and hypotonic. Hyper is the higher osmotic pressure, hypo is the lower one.
steps.memory_tip: Hyper is higher, hypo is lower, iso is equal.
steps.margin_note: One example is enough for this mark. The hypertonic and hypotonic pair is the usual follow-up part, so write it here.

insider_note: Blood with 0.9% (w/v) NaCl is the example every examiner expects. Write the figure and the (w/v), not just the word saline.
